analysis.one_liner: Requires farm employers to protect farmworkers from wildfire smoke and dangerous heat.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past a Senate committee referral, dying without a single cosponsor or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created an immediate federal workplace safety rule requiring agricultural employers to give farmworkers N95 or N100 respirators when wildfire smoke makes the air dangerous, and water, shade, cooling facilities, and rest breaks when heat reaches dangerous levels. Employers would also have to train workers, in a language they understand, on how to use the equipment and recognize heat illness. The Labor Department would then have written a permanent standard at least as protective as the strongest state rule. The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced and received no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmworkers — an estimated 2 to 3 million people, many of them immigrants working outdoors — gain protection from two hazards that kill: wildfire smoke, which the bill's findings note has lengthened wildfire season by over two months since the 1970s, and extreme heat, which killed more than 100 people in Oregon's June 2021 heat wave, including a farmworker. The equipment, water, shade, and mandatory rest breaks would apply precisely when air quality or heat reaches dangerous levels, and workers could not be fired for asserting these rights under existing anti-retaliation law.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Farmworkers exposed to smoke and heat

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes smoke protection (N95 or N100 certified respirators) and heat protection (water and cooling facilities) mandatory employer-provided equipment when conditions reach levels the Secretary of Labor deems dangerous, and mandatory use at extremely dangerous levels.
Once dangerous conditions hit, workers must get rest breaks of at least 10 minutes every 2 hours in shaded areas with reduced smoke or heat exposure.

Employers must provide training materials in a language the worker understands — including indigenous languages — covering equipment use, how long protection lasts, the health effects of smoke inhalation, and the signs of heat illness, with a chance to ask questions.

The standard would be enforced like any OSHA workplace standard, including the ban on retaliating against workers who assert their rights, and the Labor Department must provide compliance help and sample training materials to employers.

analysis.who_pays: Agricultural employers, who would bear the cost of buying and maintaining respirators, providing water, shade and cooling equipment, and paying for mandatory rest breaks during dangerous conditions — costs that fall hardest on smaller farm operations. Consumers could see some of the cost passed through in food prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Farm employers buying equipment and rest time

drawbacks.text: The compliance costs land on farm operators, including small growers, who must supply respirators, cooling facilities, and paid rest breaks during dangerous conditions, and those costs can be passed to consumers through food prices.

Requiring respirators only when air quality is already dangerous addresses symptoms rather than root causes, and masks provide limited protection during heavy exertion in extreme heat, a limitation an honest supporter would acknowledge.

The bill demands a permanent OSHA standard within about 90 days of enactment — a rulemaking process that normally takes far longer — and enforcement against thousands of dispersed, seasonal worksites would be difficult in practice.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is direct and life-saving for a workforce with one of the highest heat-death rates in the country, against a cost of equipment and break time that farming operations already manage in the states (California, Washington, Oregon) that have adopted similar rules. The bill even includes compliance assistance for employers. The main honest objections are the tight rulemaking timeline and the difficulty of enforcing rules at remote worksites, not the underlying value of the protections.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate HELP Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Merkley introduced the bill on September 15, 2021, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
No other senator signed on as a cosponsor — the cosponsor list shows zero.
The action history shows no further steps after the committee referral: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

The bill's findings section documented the stakes: wildfire season has grown by more than two months since the 1970s, and more than 100 people died in Oregon's June 2021 heat wave, including a farmworker.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Agricultural employers are better off: no federal equipment, water, shade, or rest-break requirements were imposed, and no new OSHA standard was written for farmworkers, who remain without a federal smoke or heat protection rule.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Farm employers avoiding new safety mandates

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oregon; sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Farmworker Smoke and Excessive Heat Protection Act and referred it to committee, after his state's June 2021 heat wave killed more than 100 people, including a farmworker.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Patty Murray (D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and took no recorded action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: The Senate
against.what_they_did: Never considered the bill; it never left committee or appeared on any floor calendar.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never attracted a second sponsor of either party — zero cosponsors — so the record shows no partisan split, only an absence of support beyond the sponsor.

industries.industry: Agricultural employers (farms and growers employing farmworkers)
industries.note: The bill would have required them to buy respirators, provide water, shade and cooling, and give paid rest breaks during dangerous smoke and heat, with training costs on top. Its death leaves their labor costs unchanged, while workers continue to bear the health risks.
A federal mandate for NIOSH-certified N95/N100 respirators for farmworkers would have created a new customer base for certified protective equipment; without the bill, that demand never materializes.
